title: Basic Coagulation Testing: PT/INR & aPTT

references.label: Standard clinical hematology laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: Prothrombin Time (PT, reported with an INR) and activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) are the two most common screening coagulation tests, each probing a different arm of the clotting cascade.
explanation: Both tests measure the time (in seconds) for citrated plasma to clot after specific reagents are added, but they trigger clotting through different pathways: PT is triggered by adding tissue factor (thromboplastin) plus calcium, primarily reflecting the extrinsic and common pathways (factors including VII, X, V, II/prothrombin, and fibrinogen) — clinically most associated with monitoring vitamin K antagonist (e.g. warfarin) therapy, where the INR (International Normalized Ratio) standardizes PT results across different thromboplastin reagents/instruments so results are comparable between laboratories. aPTT is triggered by adding a contact activator plus phospholipid and calcium, primarily reflecting the intrinsic and common pathways (including factors VIII, IX, XI, XII) — clinically most associated with monitoring unfractionated heparin therapy and screening for certain factor deficiencies or inhibitors. Both tests depend critically on correct sample collection: the sodium citrate tube's 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio (see the related anticoagulant/tube concept) must be met, since under-filling introduces relative excess citrate that falsely prolongs both results.

comparison.left: PT/INR: monitoring warfarin/vitamin K antagonist therapy

commonMisconceptions: Assuming a prolonged PT or aPTT always means a bleeding risk from factor deficiency — it can also reflect an anticoagulant drug effect, a lupus-type inhibitor, or a specimen collection error (e.g. under-filled citrate tube), which must be distinguished before clinical interpretation.
